title: RoY 2026 Investment Team Priorities v1 (SPC internal deck) — slide 8: AI Native Industrial Production
author: SPC investment team
summary: SPC rest-of-year 2026 priorities deck. Slide 8 defines AI-native industrial production: companies that build and run their own production capacity with in-house AI/software/robotics and sell parts or material, vs software-first platforms that run plants owned by others. Five layers (metals supply, fabrication, precision parts, materials R&D, factory AI) with incumbents, upstart angle and example startups. Thesis: demand for domestic production is structural; owning the plant turns production into proprietary data; moats are process data, secured capacity/permits, customer qualification; hardware-inclusive producers are in scope if output is mission-critical and there is a software loop.

key_facts.fact: US manufacturing may need 3.8M more workers by 2033; 1.9M could go unfilled
key_facts.quote: per Deloitte and the Manufacturing Institute

key_facts.fact: US installed 34,200 industrial robots in 2024 vs 295,000 in China
Top refiner holds 72% average share of key energy minerals; China ~85% of rare earth refining
Size: ~$1.3T/yr US manufacturing worker earnings (12.6M x ~$107K); ~$200B US metals distribution; $6.5T production outside China exposed to rare earth supply cuts

takeaways: Two approaches: owner-operators (1872, Nox, Mariana) vs software-first (Arda)
Data that only exists by running physical production is the moat claim (1872 Factory OS)
Hardware-inclusive producers in scope: judge by size of system compounded, not early gross margin
Several startup valuations on the slide are stale vs Harmonic as of 2026-10-22 (see companies/*.md data_quality)
